title: SPX101 Week 5: Measurement Quality (Validity, Reliability & Error)
description: 40 teacher-approved questions on true score vs error, random vs systematic error, face/content/construct/criterion validity, Bland-Altman plots, intra/inter-rater reliability, sampling rate, and hysteresis.
approvedBy: SPX101 Teaching Team (Static Course Snapshot v1.1.0)

questions.learningOutcome: Use the core model: observed score equals true score plus error
questions.stem: According to the foundational measurement model in SPX101 Week 5, how is any observed test score related to the athlete's true score?

options.text: Observed score equals the true physiological score plus measurement error
Observed score is always identical to the true score on digital devices
Observed score equals the true score multiplied by the sample size
True score is only present when a test is performed inside a laboratory

questions.explanation: Every measurement is an estimate filtered through an imperfect process: Observed Score = True Score + Error.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Core Measurement Model

questions.learningOutcome: Explain why reliability is essential for validity but does not guarantee correctness by itself
questions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the relationship between reliability and validity in sport and clinical measurement?

options.text: A test can be reliable without being valid, but cannot be valid without being reliable
A test can be valid even when its results vary wildly and randomly every trial
Any test that produces consistent numbers is automatically valid for every purpose
Reliability and validity have no mathematical or practical connection

questions.explanation: Using the archery bullseye analogy, arrows clustered tightly off-target are reliable (consistent) but not valid; however, you cannot consistently hit the bullseye (valid) without consistency (reliability).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Reliability and Validity

questions.learningOutcome: Define validity and distinguish face, content, construct, and criterion validity in applied testing
questions.stem: When a test simply 'looks like' it measures what it is supposed to measure to an observer or athlete, which form of validity is being described?

options.text: Face validity
Criterion validity
Construct validity
Inter-rater reliability

questions.explanation: Face validity refers to whether a test superficially appears to measure the intended target, which is a starting point rather than proof of accuracy.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Types of Validity

questions.learningOutcome: Define validity and distinguish face, content, construct, and criterion validity in applied testing
questions.stem: Why does the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test demonstrate strong content validity for assessing functional mobility in patients with Parkinson's disease?

options.text: It includes standing, walking, and a 180-degree turn that commonly triggers gait freezing
It requires a 100-metre maximal sprint over hurdles on an outdoor track
It compares a laser sensor against a twelve-camera 3D motion capture lab
It directly measures dopamine neurotransmitter concentrations in the brain

questions.explanation: Content validity asks whether a test covers all relevant dimensions of the task; for Parkinson's patients, the TUG captures rising, walking, sitting, and the critical turning component.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Content Validity

questions.learningOutcome: Define validity and distinguish face, content, construct, and criterion validity in applied testing
questions.stem: How do researchers establish criterion validity when evaluating a newly developed wearable or optical sensor?

options.text: By comparing the new tool's outputs directly against an established gold-standard measure
By asking undergraduate students whether the sensor casing looks modern
By testing the new sensor twice without comparing it to any reference device
By pricing the sensor higher than competing devices on the commercial market

questions.explanation: Criterion validity tests how closely a new measurement tool agrees with an established gold-standard (criterion) reference.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Criterion Validity

questions.learningOutcome: Explain why strong correlation alone does not prove measurement equivalence
questions.stem: Why can two measurement devices show a very high correlation (or ICC) and yet NOT be interchangeable in practice?

options.text: One device may have a consistent systematic offset (bias) higher or lower than the other
A correlation near 1.00 means the two devices have zero linear relationship
High correlation only occurs when both devices are turned off during testing
Correlation measures battery life rather than whether scores rise and fall together

questions.explanation: Correlation tracks whether scores rise and fall together; if Device B always reads 0.3 m/s faster than Device A, correlation is perfect (1.0) despite a systematic bias shown on a Bland-Altman plot.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Beyond Correlation & Bland-Altman Plots

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret criterion-validation outputs including ICC/correlation, mean absolute error, and Bland-Altman patterns
questions.stem: If a gold-standard 3D camera records a walking speed of 1.10 m/s and a LiDAR sensor records 1.20 m/s on that trial, what is the absolute error?

options.text: 0.10 m/s (the magnitude of difference between the two devices)
1.15 m/s (the average speed across the two devices)
2.30 m/s (the sum of the two recorded speeds)
0.00 m/s because both devices measured forward walking

questions.explanation: Absolute error on a trial is the magnitude of difference between the new tool and the criterion reference: |1.20 - 1.10| = 0.10 m/s.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Mean Absolute Error

questions.learningOutcome: Apply context-based validity reasoning across different tasks, speeds, and measurement intervals
questions.stem: In the LiDAR validation study, why did the 3-metre timing interval outperform the 0.5-metre flying-run interval?

options.text: Over very short, high-speed intervals, small timing or position errors are heavily magnified
Laser beams cannot travel less than three metres through indoor laboratory air
Participants walked backward during all three-metre trials in the study
The 3D motion-capture cameras were switched off during the 0.5-metre trials

questions.explanation: Over a 0.5 m flying sprint, total transit time is tiny, so any small boundary noise creates a much larger percentage error (worse signal-to-noise ratio) than over a 3 m interval.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2 & Part 4: Signal-to-Noise and Interval Length

questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate whether a tool measures the intended construct rather than only appearing plausible
questions.stem: What serious clinical risk can arise from applying a submaximal VO2max prediction equation validated on young adults to an older cardiac rehabilitation patient?

options.text: It may overestimate true aerobic capacity and clear the patient for unsafe exercise intensity
It converts heart rate into bone density units that cannot be read by cardiologists
Prediction equations work identically across all ages, diseases, and medications
Submaximal equations physically interfere with hospital pacemaker batteries

questions.explanation: Validity is population-specific; using a young-adult equation on an older cardiac patient can overestimate VO2max (e.g., by 8 mL/kg/min) and lead to unsafe exercise prescription.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Clinical Consequences of Invalid Tools

questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish test-retest, intra-rater, inter-rater, and inter-device reliability
questions.stem: When two different physiotherapists independently score the same patient's gait video and their scores are compared, which reliability type is being evaluated?

options.text: Inter-rater reliability
Intra-rater reliability
Inter-device reliability
Face validity

questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability measures consistency between two or more different assessors scoring the same performance.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Forms of Reliability

questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish test-retest, intra-rater, inter-rater, and inter-device reliability
questions.stem: What distinguishes intra-rater reliability from inter-rater reliability in movement screening?

options.text: Intra-rater examines whether the same assessor gives consistent scores across repeated scorings
Intra-rater requires at least thirty different clinicians from separate hospitals
Intra-rater compares two different brands of force platforms under mechanical load
Intra-rater compares a stopwatch against a 3D motion-capture camera system

questions.explanation: Intra-rater reliability evaluates consistency within a single assessor across repeated scorings, whereas inter-rater evaluates agreement across different assessors.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Intra-Rater vs Inter-Rater

questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate common inter-rater challenges in subjective coaching and clinical scoring
questions.stem: Why did collapsing the clinical gait impairment scale from five categories (0–4) into a binary classification (impaired vs unimpaired) improve accuracy and agreement?

options.text: Overly fine scales can introduce 'false precision' and greater disagreement between raters
Computers cannot store numbers larger than one in machine-learning models
All participants with acquired brain injury suddenly recovered during the study
Binary scales double the frame rate of standard smartphone video cameras

questions.explanation: Granular subjective scales (like 0–100 or 0–4 with subtle boundaries) often create false precision and rater disagreement, whereas well-defined simpler categories improve reliability.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: False Precision and Category Collapsing

questions.learningOutcome: Use the gait machine-learning case example to discuss reducing assessor variability
questions.stem: Why do reliability researchers use statistics like weighted kappa when evaluating agreement between clinical raters?

options.text: It quantifies agreement between raters beyond what would be expected by random chance alone
It adjusts the patient's walking speed for the weight of their shoes and clothing
It corrects load-cell voltage drift caused by warm summer laboratory temperatures
It converts a 10 Hz sampling rate into an 80 Hz sampling rate automatically

questions.explanation: Even random guessing produces some coincidental agreement; weighted kappa measures inter-rater agreement above and beyond chance.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Judging Consistency with Weighted Kappa

questions.learningOutcome: Differentiate random and systematic error and describe how each affects interpretation
questions.stem: How does systematic measurement error differ from random measurement error?

options.text: Systematic error pushes measurements consistently in one direction; random error fluctuates unpredictably
Systematic error changes direction every millisecond; random error is a fixed constant offset
Random error only occurs on broken devices, whereas systematic error cannot be measured
Systematic error and random error are two names for the exact same phenomenon

questions.explanation: Random error is unpredictable noise oscillating around the signal, whereas systematic error is a consistent directional bias or offset (e.g., always reading faster or heavier).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Random vs Systematic Error

questions.learningOutcome: Identify common error sources across instrument, procedural, biological, and sampling factors
questions.stem: In the context of load cells and force platforms, what is hysteresis?

options.text: Failure of the sensor reading to return immediately to the same baseline after load is removed
The maximum knee flexion angle achieved during a counter-movement vertical jump
Loss of wireless Bluetooth packets when a participant walks behind a brick wall
Disagreement between two coaches rating the same athlete's shooting technique

questions.explanation: Hysteresis occurs when a sensor's output differs during loading versus unloading (or fails to return cleanly to zero baseline after a load is applied and removed).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Hysteresis and Instrument Error

questions.learningOutcome: Identify common error sources across instrument, procedural, biological, and sampling factors
questions.stem: A scale reads 10 kg when a 10 kg mass is placed on it, 20 kg for 20 kg, but only 25 kg when 30 kg is applied. Which instrument error is present?

options.text: Non-linearity across the measurement range
Inter-rater subjective scoring bias
Circadian biological rhythm variability
Lack of superficial face validity

questions.explanation: Linearity requires equal increments of mechanical load to produce proportional increments in sensor output across the full operating range.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Non-Linearity in Force Testing

questions.learningOutcome: Explain how task speed and sampling rate influence error in dynamic measurements
questions.stem: Why did the modified bathroom scales show slightly greater error during rapid sit-to-stand tasks than during slow weight shifts at their default 10 Hz setting?

options.text: Sampling only 10 times per second can miss rapid force peaks during fast movements
Standing up quickly shuts off the electrical battery inside digital scales
Human body mass permanently doubles whenever a person performs a sit-to-stand
Laboratory force plates cannot record vertical force during sitting movements

questions.explanation: A 10 Hz sampling rate (10 samples/s) is sufficient for static or slow weight shifts, but fast dynamic tasks require higher sampling (e.g., 80 Hz) to capture rapid force changes accurately.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Sampling Rate and Movement Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret practical error indicators such as mean absolute error and signal-to-noise behaviour
questions.stem: In the bathroom scale validation study, why did observers notice small weight additions sooner on the modified scale trace than on the lab force plate trace?

options.text: The modified scales had lower baseline signal noise, making subtle force changes easier to see
The laboratory force plate trace was invisible on the projector screen
The observers were told in advance which trace belonged to the bathroom scale
The laboratory force plate was disconnected from its amplifier during the test

questions.explanation: High-capacity lab impact plates had more baseline oscillation (noise), whereas the modified bathroom scales had a cleaner baseline (higher signal-to-noise ratio for small loads).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Signal Noise in Force Traces

questions.learningOutcome: Identify common error sources across instrument, procedural, biological, and sampling factors
questions.stem: How can testing athletes in winter and re-testing them in a hot summer gym with temperature-sensitive load cells distort research conclusions?

options.text: Thermal drift in the sensor can create an artificial score change mistaken for a training effect
Earth's gravitational pull is twenty percent stronger during summer months
Heat automatically increases the criterion validity of uncalibrated strain gauges
Temperature only affects wooden rulers and never affects electronic load cells

questions.explanation: Heat and electrical warm-up can cause load-cell calibration drift, inflating or distorting observed effect sizes if attributed to the athlete rather than the instrument.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Flawed Research and Instrument Error

questions.learningOutcome: Apply protocol controls to improve repeatability across sessions
questions.stem: Why do sport scientists standardize the time of day, hydration status, and prior exercise before repeating a performance test?

options.text: To minimize biological variability such as circadian rhythm and acute fatigue
To eliminate electronic hysteresis inside the plastic timing gate reflectors
To change an intra-rater study into a criterion validity study
To prevent analog-to-digital integer rounding inside the computer processor

questions.explanation: Circadian rhythm, hydration, and residual fatigue are biological error sources that vary from day to day; standardizing test conditions improves test-retest reliability.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Biological Factors in Measurement Error

questions.learningOutcome: Connect measurement quality to load monitoring, triage, and progression decisions
questions.stem: An athlete runs 100 km in a week. A valid GPS unit (±2% error) reads 98–102 km, whereas a poor unit (±15% error) reads 85–115 km. What is the practical risk of the poor unit?

options.text: It can mask overload or falsely suggest fatigue, leading to under-recovery or suboptimal training
A 15% GPS error makes the athlete physically run 15 km backwards during matches
Distance error has no effect on how coaches plan weekly training volume
Both units are equally fit for fine-tuning elite weekly running prescriptions

questions.explanation: A ±15% distance error (30 km uncertainty band on 100 km) can cause staff to push an already overloaded athlete into injury or hold back an athlete who needs stimulus.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: GPS Tracking Error Example

questions.learningOutcome: Use error-aware reasoning when deciding if change is meaningful
questions.stem: What does the Week 5 NBA Draft Combine vertical jump interactive demonstrate about traditional reach-and-slap jump measurement?

options.text: Measurement error in standing reach and jump vanes can substantially reorder athlete rankings
Mechanical slap-vane devices have zero measurement error to the nearest micrometre
Vertical jump height depends only on shoe colour and never on lower-body impulse
NBA teams never record vertical jump scores during pre-draft evaluations

questions.explanation: Traditional combine jump testing contains enough measurement error (including standing-reach manipulation and vane spacing) to scramble athlete rankings when small differences separate players.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P451] Week 5.2 Knowledge Interactive: NBA Draft Jump Error

questions.learningOutcome: Make fit-for-purpose decisions by judging whether uncertainty is acceptable for the use case
questions.stem: Since no measurement instrument has zero error, what is the central question a practitioner must ask before using a tool?

options.text: Is the level of measurement uncertainty small enough for the specific decision I need to make?
Can I wait until an instrument with absolute zero error is invented before testing?
Is this tool the most expensive model listed in the laboratory catalogue?
Can I ignore measurement error as long as I report numbers to four decimal places?

questions.explanation: Because every tool contains some error, professional judgment rests on whether the tool is 'fit for purpose'—meaning its error is smaller than the change or threshold that matters.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Fit-for-Purpose Decisions

questions.learningOutcome: Use the gait machine-learning case example to discuss reducing assessor variability
questions.stem: In the Week 5 clinical gait study of participants with acquired brain injury, what caused the involuntary elbow flexion ('associated reaction') during walking?

options.text: Motor overflow during the effort of walking stimulated involuntary biceps contraction
Participants were instructed to carry a heavy dumbbell in their left hand
The laboratory temperature was kept below freezing to induce shivering
Clinicians tied the participant's arm in a sling before recording video

questions.explanation: In patients with acquired brain injury, relatively high-effort tasks like walking can trigger motor overflow (an associated reaction) that stimulates involuntary upper-limb flexion.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Machine Learning and Clinical Gait Scoring

questions.learningOutcome: Use the gait machine-learning case example to discuss reducing assessor variability
questions.stem: What was the main clinical benefit of training a pose-tracking machine-learning model on ratings from three expert physiotherapists?

options.text: It provided consistent expert-level scoring across clinics without individual rater drift
It cured acquired brain injuries without requiring physical rehabilitation
It proved that human clinicians always agree 100% of the time on 5-point scales
It measured ground reaction force in newtons without needing any camera

questions.explanation: Because even expert clinicians show only moderate inter-rater agreement, an automated pose-tracking model acts like a consistent 'expert in your pocket' across hospitals and regional clinics.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Machine Learning Case Study Findings

questions.learningOutcome: Apply protocol controls to improve repeatability across sessions
questions.stem: When human observation is required for movement screening or technique scoring, which strategy best improves inter-rater reliability?

options.text: Use clearly defined scoring criteria, rater training, and simpler category boundaries
Expand the rating scale from five points to one hundred unanchored points
Let each coach invent their own private criteria during the testing session
Wait three weeks after the session to score the athlete from memory

questions.explanation: Clear operational criteria, standardized rater training, and avoiding overly granular scales reduce subjective interpretation differences between raters.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Reducing Variation in Reliability

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret criterion-validation outputs including ICC/correlation, mean absolute error, and Bland-Altman patterns
questions.stem: On a Bland-Altman plot comparing two speed sensors, what does a mean difference line sitting close to 0.00 indicate?

options.text: Minimal systematic bias on average between the two measurement systems
Zero correlation between the speeds recorded by the two systems
Both sensors recorded a speed of 0.00 m/s for every participant
Infinite random error across all walking and running velocities

questions.explanation: In a Bland-Altman plot, the central horizontal line represents the mean difference (bias) between devices; a mean near zero indicates little systematic offset between them.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Bland-Altman Plots

questions.learningOutcome: Identify common error sources across instrument, procedural, biological, and sampling factors
questions.stem: Why is manual stopwatch timing particularly unreliable for short sprints or 4-metre clinical walk tests?

options.text: Human thumb reaction time at start and finish is large relative to the short total duration
Digital smartphone crystals lose several minutes over a four-second period
Light travels too slowly across a four-metre room for human vision
Stopwatches only function outdoors when connected to GPS satellites

questions.explanation: Human visual judgment and thumb reaction time at both the start line and finish line introduce substantial error relative to a short 3–4 second test window.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Stopwatch Error in Short Tests

questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish test-retest, intra-rater, inter-rater, and inter-device reliability
questions.stem: In the Bunnings bathroom scale study, testing two units of the $10 model and two units of the $30 model under identical loads evaluated which property?

options.text: Inter-device consistency across units and models
Intra-rater subjective video scoring consistency
Superficial face validity of aerobic endurance
Circadian variation in human core temperature

questions.explanation: Comparing multiple physical units and models under the same mechanical loads tests inter-device reliability (consistency across equipment units).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Inter-Device Consistency

questions.learningOutcome: Define validity and distinguish face, content, construct, and criterion validity in applied testing
questions.stem: What does construct validity evaluate when developing a physical performance or clinical assessment?

options.text: Whether the test score statistically reflects the underlying theoretical trait or capacity
Whether the testing frame is constructed from stainless steel rather than aluminium
Whether a casual observer thinks the test looks impressive at first glance
Whether the same assessor gets the same score when re-watching a video clip

questions.explanation: Construct validity assesses whether a test genuinely reflects the underlying theoretical construct (e.g., functional physical capacity or agility) it is intended to represent.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Construct Validity

questions.learningOutcome: Apply protocol controls to improve repeatability across sessions
questions.stem: Why do testing protocols often record three or more trials on the same day and average them when a measure has modest trial-to-trial random error?

options.text: Averaging repeated trials helps cancel out random positive and negative fluctuations
Averaging ten trials automatically fixes a miscalibrated scale with a +5 kg offset
Performing multiple trials eliminates the need to calibrate the instrument
Averaging turns a cycling test into a valid test of basketball shooting skill

questions.explanation: Because random error fluctuates up and down around the true score, averaging multiple trials reduces random noise (though it does not remove systematic bias).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3 & Week 9.3: Multiple Trials and Random Error

questions.learningOutcome: Use error-aware reasoning when deciding if change is meaningful
questions.stem: If a strength device has high random measurement error, what risk arises when comparing an athlete's left leg against their right leg?

options.text: Random noise between the two tests may be misread as a real limb strength asymmetry
High random error guarantees both limbs will record the exact same newton value
The device will only measure the dominant leg and refuse to test the other side
High measurement error accelerates tendon healing in the weaker limb

questions.explanation: Testing the left limb and then the right limb with a noisy instrument can produce different numbers purely from measurement error, creating a false impression of asymmetry.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Why Measurement Error Matters for Asymmetry

questions.topic: Sampling Rate in GPS Agile Movement
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how task speed and sampling rate influence error in dynamic measurements
questions.stem: Why can a low-frequency GPS unit fail to capture the true peak speed of an athlete performing rapid, sharp agility cuts?

options.text: Brief velocity peaks and direction changes occur between samples and get smoothed out
Agility cones block radio waves from reaching the athlete's GPS vest
Athletes move slower than 0.1 m/s whenever they change direction on grass
Low sampling rate makes the GPS vest physically heavier on the athlete's back

questions.explanation: During rapid acceleration and sharp cuts, if sampling frequency is too low relative to movement speed, brief peak velocities and path curvature between sample points are missed.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1 & Part 4: Sampling Factors in Dynamic Movement

questions.learningOutcome: Identify common error sources across instrument, procedural, biological, and sampling factors
questions.stem: How does converting a continuous physical signal into whole numbers (integers) inside a digital device introduce measurement error?

options.text: Rounding continuous values to discrete digital steps introduces quantization/rounding error
Digital numbers always drift upward by ten percent every hour
Integer conversion depends on the assessor's subjective coaching bias
Rounding to whole numbers increases precision to infinite decimal places

questions.explanation: Hardware digitization rounds continuous physical quantities into discrete steps or integers, introducing small hardware resolution error.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Hardware Limitations and Digitization

questions.learningOutcome: Recognise the practical consequences of poor measurement, including misclassification and inappropriate decisions
questions.stem: How can using an insensitive or high-error test harm a patient who has genuinely improved during a six-week rehabilitation program?

options.text: The noisy tool may show no gain or a worse score, discouraging the patient from continuing
Insensitive tools always double the patient's recorded strength on re-testing
Measurement error directly causes acute ligament inflammation during rest
Patients never care about their test results during clinical rehabilitation

questions.explanation: If a tool has excessive error or poor sensitivity, a patient who worked hard for six weeks may appear unchanged or worse, causing frustration and drop-out.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Rehabilitation Milestones and Error

questions.learningOutcome: Apply context-based validity reasoning across different tasks, speeds, and measurement intervals
questions.stem: Why did the authors of the 3-metre laboratory LiDAR study caution against immediately assuming the sensor was validated for 40-metre outdoor sprints?

options.text: Validation evidence only covers the tested capture volume (3 m) and population until tested further
Lasers travel at different speeds when sprints are longer than ten metres
Outdoor sprinting uses different mathematical equations for velocity than indoor running
40-metre sprints do not involve acceleration or maximal running velocity

questions.explanation: Validity is bounded by the conditions tested: validating a sensor over a 3 m laboratory capture volume in healthy adults does not automatically prove accuracy at 40 m or in clinical groups without dedicated testing.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2: Study Limitations and Validation Scope

questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate common inter-rater challenges in subjective coaching and clinical scoring
questions.stem: A patient is scored on a subjective movement screen by Clinician A in Week 1 and by Clinician B in Week 6. Why is interpreting the change difficult?

options.text: True patient change is confounded with inter-rater scoring differences between the two clinicians
Having two clinicians eliminates all random and systematic measurement error
Movement screens cannot be repeated more than once per calendar year
Clinician B always scores higher than Clinician A on objective force plates

questions.explanation: When different assessors score pre- and post-intervention on a subjective scale with modest inter-rater reliability, an apparent improvement or decline may simply reflect assessor differences.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 3: Real-World Inter-Rater Challenges

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret practical error indicators such as mean absolute error and signal-to-noise behaviour
questions.stem: Why was it necessary to test the modified bathroom scales under both calibrated static weights AND dynamic sit-to-stand movements?

options.text: A scale accurate for steady static mass may still lag or lose accuracy during dynamic force changes
Static weights only test sampling rate, whereas sit-to-stands only test battery life
Bathroom scales are never used with human participants standing on them
Static accuracy mathematically guarantees 1000 Hz dynamic impact accuracy

questions.explanation: Consumer scales are built to measure steady static weight; clinical rehab tasks like weight-shifting and sit-to-stands involve time-varying forces, requiring dedicated dynamic validation.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4: Static vs Dynamic Validation

questions.learningOutcome: Apply three core checks before trusting data: validity, reliability, and acceptable error
questions.stem: Before trusting any measurement tool in sport or clinical practice, which three foundational checks does Week 5 Part 1 require?

options.text: Is the tool valid, is it reliable, and is the measurement error small enough for the decision?
Is the tool wireless, does it have a colour screen, and is it endorsed by an athlete?
Was it built in a lab, does it use lasers, and does it export PDF reports?
Does it measure heart rate, does it measure jump height, and is it waterproof?

questions.explanation: The three pillars of measurement quality are validity (measuring the right thing), reliability (reproducible under consistent conditions), and acceptable error for the intended decision.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Three Core Checks

questions.learningOutcome: Identify common error sources across instrument, procedural, biological, and sampling factors
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a procedural error source rather than an instrument hardware error?

options.text: Inconsistent tester instructions or changing floor surface and footwear between sessions
Thermal hysteresis in a strain-gauge amplifier after two hours of electrical warm-up
Analog-to-digital integer quantization inside a microcontroller chip
Mechanical non-linearity of a spring transducer above 500 newtons

questions.explanation: Procedural error arises from how the test is administered—such as inconsistent instructions, tester technique, footwear, or surface conditions—and is controlled through strict protocol adherence.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 1: Procedural Sources of Error
